projects.name: Sector
projects.title: What ate my disk?
projects.lead: A native macOS disk analyzer and cleaner. Its own parallel scanner walks two million files **5× faster than du**, with byte-identical totals.

media.alt: Sector: zooming into a folder on the disk map, switching between rings and tiles

showcase.task: Scan ~/projects · 2.06 M files and folders · M4 Pro

specs.label: for 2 million files; du takes 30.7
to load the last scan at launch
for a 2-million-node tree
lines of network code. Nothing leaves the Mac.

case.summary: A disk analyzer and cleaner for macOS 26, in Swift 6 and SwiftUI. It finds what is taking the space, shows it as rings or tiles, and gets it back **through the Trash, with undo**.

sections.title: A scanner built for speed
body: Scanning `~/projects`, 2.06 million files and folders, takes 6.5 seconds; `du -sk` needs 30.7 for the same folder and arrives at the same total.
bullets: `getattrlistbulk(2)` returns a whole directory's attributes in a few syscalls instead of one `stat` per file.
Worker threads share a depth-first work stack and open each directory with `openat` relative to its parent.
A directory's children are committed in one batch, so they sit together and always after their parent: rolling sizes up is **a single reverse pass**.
Hard links count once, mount points are skipped, so `/` never wanders into external drives.

sections.title: Two million nodes, cheaply
body: The tree is a structure of arrays, about 35 bytes a node plus names: 117 MB for two million. The last scan is saved to disk and loads in 10 ms, so the app opens instantly and refreshes in the background.

sections.title: What it finds
bullets: **Disk Map**: rings and tiles from precomputed geometry; click a segment to fly into a folder.
**Smart Clean**: Xcode caches, stale `node_modules`, unused Docker images, old simulators, app caches and logs, in one pass.
**Duplicates**: size, then a partial hash, then full SHA-256. APFS clones are recognised, so the number is what deleting really frees.
**Apps**: every app with its hidden data in `~/Library`, to remove completely or just reset.

sections.title: Safe by default
body: Everything goes to the Trash first, and History puts files back where they were for 30 days. Cleanup never follows a symlink out of its target, never crosses a mount point and refuses anything less than two levels inside your home folder.

sections.title: Stack
body: Swift 6 and SwiftUI with Liquid Glass, a UI-free engine package covered by tests, WidgetKit for two desktop widgets, a menu bar extra. English and Russian.

projects.name: LarpGuard
projects.title: Cloudflare.
projects.lead: A bot filter in front of Traefik that reads **every layer** of a connection and asks one question: does this stack match the browser it claims to be?

specs.label: layers fingerprinted: TCP, TLS, HTTP/2, QUIC
gradient-boosting inference in C++
prefilter with its own loader
proxy lists. RTT does the work.

points: TCP SYN, JA4/JA4T/JA4H, HTTP/2 and QUIC fingerprints scored into human, suspicious, bot and verified_bot
Proxy detection from the RTT gap between TCP and the TLS 1.3 handshake, without proxy lists
XDP/eBPF prefilter with its own loader; gradient-boosting inference in C++ in microseconds

case.summary: A bot filter I run in front of my own servers. Faking a User-Agent takes one line; faking a browser's TCP handshake, TLS hello, HTTP/2 settings and header order all at once is another story. LarpGuard checks that **the whole stack agrees**.

facts.label: from the kernel to the dashboard

sections.title: Why build it
body: Bots lie about who they are, and the commercial answer is a black box sitting in front of all your traffic. I wanted the same depth of inspection on my own servers, with rules I can read and data that stays with me.

sections.title: Every layer, one question
body: Each connection is fingerprinted on every layer it passes through, and the fingerprints are checked against each other: does this stack match the browser the client claims to be?
bullets: **TCP SYN**: window size, option order and TTL, before a single byte of TLS.
**TLS**: JA4, JA4T and JA4H, read straight from the ClientHello.
**HTTP/2 and QUIC**: SETTINGS frames, pseudo-header order, transport parameters.
A consistency score sorts every client into `human`, `suspicious`, `bot` or `verified_bot`.

sections.title: Proxies without proxy lists
body: A proxy adds a hop, and a hop shows up as time. LarpGuard compares the round trip of the TCP handshake with the round trip of the TLS 1.3 handshake; when they disagree, someone is in the middle. No IP lists to buy or keep fresh.

sections.title: The fast path lives in the kernel
body: Known-bad traffic never reaches userspace: an XDP/eBPF prefilter with its own loader (no libbpf) drops it at the network card. Honeypot paths, a tarpit and decoy responses waste the time of whoever is left.

sections.title: It learns from its own traffic
body: Every decision is an event in ClickHouse. A gradient-boosting model is trained on those events and runs inside the C++ gateway in microseconds. The grey zone gets a JS challenge with proof of work and my own CAPTCHA; real crawlers are verified by DNS and IP ranges, and Web Bot Auth signatures (Ed25519).

sections.title: Rules people can read
body: Policies are written in a small rule language, and rate limits use GCRA kept in sync across instances through Valkey.
sections.code:
path ~ "/admin*" and class != "human" => challenge
ja4 in known_bad => drop
rate(ip, 100/min) => tarpit

sections.title: Stack
body: C++20, BoringSSL, HTTP/3 on ngtcp2 and nghttp3, XDP/BPF, ClickHouse, Valkey, behind Traefik.

RBAC admin: Argon2id, passkeys, TOTP, OIDC, 6 roles, audit log

case.summary: My own VPN business, turned into an open platform: the Telegram bot customers buy from, the billing behind it, support, marketing and an admin panel, all on top of Remnawave, **without owning Xray**.

sections.title: Why open it up
body: Running a VPN service is mostly not about VPN: it is plans, payments, refunds, support and a bot people actually enjoy using. Every Remnawave operator rebuilds that glue. Omniflow is the glue, done once and properly.

sections.title: A whole shop inside Telegram
bullets: A plan catalogue with purchase, renewal and upgrade.
Payments through **Telegram Stars**, **CryptoBot** and **YooKassa**.
Promo codes, a wallet, referrals and support tickets, in Russian and English.

sections.title: Money done carefully
body: Plans are immutable versions, so changing a price never rewrites what someone already paid for. Refunds and top-ups go through a wallet ledger, and access is granted through a **transactional outbox**: the payment and the job that provisions the subscription commit together, and River retries the job until Remnawave confirms it.

sections.title: An admin panel with real access control
body: Staff sign in with Argon2id passwords, passkeys, TOTP or OIDC. Six roles decide who sees what, and every action lands in an audit log.

sections.title: Stack
body: Go 1.26 with chi, pgx, sqlc and River; PostgreSQL 18, Valkey 9, OpenTelemetry; Next.js and shadcn/ui for the admin; documentation on Mintlify.

projects.name: Logical System
projects.title: Logic gates.
projects.titleDim: All the way to a computer.
projects.lead: My oldest living project: released on itch.io in 2021 (rated 4.0/5), then remastered in C++20.

examples.label: Full adder
examples.hint: Gates here count their inputs, so adding three bits takes one XOR and one AND. Flip A, B and Cin.

examples.label: RS latch
examples.hint: Two NANDs feeding each other remember. Flip S on and off, then R.

examples.label: Gates
examples.hint: NOT, AND and XOR. A signal moves one block per tick: watch it walk.

examples.label: Blinker
examples.hint: A clock flips every tick; the lamp follows three blocks behind.

specs.label: block types on an infinite grid
ticks per second, max
SUBLEQ computer, built inside
rating on itch.io

case.summary: A Turing-complete sandbox of logic gates. My oldest living project: released on itch.io in 2021 (**rated 4.0/5**), then rebuilt from scratch in C++20.

sections.title: From a school project to a remaster
body: The first version shipped when my profile still said "Java programmer from Russia". The remaster keeps the idea and rewrites everything else in modern C++.

sections.title: The simulation
bullets: 16 block types on an infinite 2D grid.
Event-driven: only what changed is recomputed, from 2 up to 65,536 ticks a second.
A signal moves one block per tick, and wires merging into one cell act as an OR.
Gates count their inputs instead of reading two fixed pins: AND is "at least two", XOR is "an odd number". So a full adder is **one XOR and one AND**.

sections.title: What people build in it
body: The examples go from an RS latch and adders to an 8-bit adder with seven-segment displays, and finally an **autonomous 16-bit SUBLEQ computer** running inside the sandbox.

sections.title: Under the hood
bullets: Instanced rendering and HDR bloom, so thousands of glowing wires stay smooth.
Undo and redo, and an autosave that survives a crash.

sections.title: Stack
body: C++20, OpenGL, ImGui and CMake.

projects.name: go-itmo
projects.title: All of ITMO.
projects.lead: Plus the full ITMO.ID login: Keycloak, PKCE, OTP, SSO and refresh-token rotation. **Dependencies: just x/oauth2 and x/net.**

items.label: routes of the BARS REST API

case.summary: An unofficial Go library for the whole ITMO ecosystem: every route of my.itmo.ru and the BARS gradebook, plus the full ITMO.ID login. **Two dependencies.**

sections.title: Why
body: Every student tool around ITMO re-implements the same login and scrapes the same pages. I wanted one typed client that does it right, so my own bots and sites could stop doing it badly.

sections.title: Coverage
bullets: All **452** routes of my.itmo.ru as **809** typed methods.
All **81** routes of the BARS REST API.

sections.title: The login, all of it
body: ITMO.ID is Keycloak. The library handles PKCE, one-time codes, single sign-on across ITMO services and refresh-token rotation, so a session just keeps working.

sections.title: Small on purpose
body: The only dependencies are `golang.org/x/oauth2` and `golang.org/x/net`.

My profile said “Java programmer from Russia” back then.

Joined GitHub in July 2018. I was about ten.
